newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: EU asks WTO to suspend panel in Cuba row with U.S..
newsitem.headline: EU asks WTO to suspend panel in Cuba row with U.S..

text.p: The European Union on Monday asked the World Trade Organisation (WTO) to suspend a panel looking into its potentially explosive row with the United States over the Helms-Burton law on investment in Cuba.

The EU move followed an agreement between the two top trade powers under which Brussels agreed to hold off on its WTO action in return for a pledge by the administration of President Bill Clinton to work for a softening of the law.

The agreement, which EU officials insist is provisional and dependent on progress in negotiations between the administration and Congress, was welcomed on Monday by WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero.

In a statement issued from Beijing where he is currently on a visit, Ruggiero said the accord on the dispute -- which trade diplomats feared could undermine the authority of the WTO -- was "a very positive development."
The agreement, he said, was also "a testimony to the effectiveness of the WTO's multilateral dispute settlement procedures in focussing the minds of participants towards a solution."

Brussels, backed by almost all the WTO's 130-state membership, argued that the law violated the organisation's open trading rules by seeking to extend the long-standing U.S. economic boycott of Cuba to other countries.
But the United States had argued the measure was a foreign policy, not a trade, matter and had indicated it would refuse to cooperate with the panel's investigation.
The EU suspension request was delivered to panel chairman Arthur Dunkel, former director-general of the WTO's predecessor, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, EU officials said.

But the short note made clear that Brussels was reserving its right to ask for the three-man body -- which had yet to hold its first formal meeting -- to be reconvened if the United States failed to carry out its side of the deal, they added.
"The EU will obviously be watching developments very carefully," one diplomatic source said.

Under the pact, shaped after months of discussion between the two top trade powers just hours before the panel was due to convene for the first time, the EU agreed to work with Washington for an accord on investment protection.

The Helms-Burton act, named for its Congressional sponsors, was partly targetted against foreign companies investing in Cuba and making use of property nationalised after President Fidel Castro came to power in 1959.

It allows for U.S. citizens, including Cubans who fled after the revolution, to take action in U.S. courts against foreigners "trafficking" in their property, and for executives of foreign firms investing in Cuba to be barred from the United States.

Clinton had already suspended implementation of the first provision, but has to win Congressional agreement to waive the second, which has already been applied to some European -- as well as Mexican and Canadian - businessman.

Under their accord, approved last week after fierce debate by ministers from the 15 EU member states, the two trade powers agreed to try to shape "disciplines and principles" on investment protection by October 15 this year.

These would be included in an overall multilateral Agreement on Investment under negotiation in the 29-nation Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), the so-called "rich man's club" of economic powers.

The disciplines should inhibit and deter firms in any state from taking up investment opportunities from a country "which has expropriated or nationalised such investments in contravention of international law," the EU-U.S. accord says.
